scenes.title: Cold open
narration: At the climax of Okinawan weddings or elections, the crowd erupts into kachāshī, a dance where men clench their fists and women flatten their palms to mimic the churning of a celebratory mixture.
This is kachāshī. 19th century to present.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (NbCWMBJ1Kk0)
Title card: kachāshī · Japan · 19th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originates from the Ryūkyū Islands, specifically Okinawa, where it has functioned for centuries as a celebratory folk tradition.
The name kachāshī comes from the Okinawan word for 'stirring,' symbolizing the mixing of people and emotions during festivities.
It is historically performed after significant events such as tegumi wrestling matches and public elections to mark victory.
on_screen: Map: Japan · East Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It is a festive dance used to celebrate weddings, harvest (Hoonen ondo), courtship (Kaadikuuu), and general success.
It serves as a communal expression of joy and a way to 'stir up' the energy of a gathering, making it a staple of Okinawan social life.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers raise their hands in the air and perform an elliptical up-and-down motion that alternates between pushing and pulling.
Men dance with fists or curled hands, while women use flat palms.
The stance is slightly bow-legged, with the feet lifting and lowering rhythmically.
Watch for The Stirring Motion.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (NbCWMBJ1Kk0)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Spontaneous group 'mixing'; no fixed formation.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is traditionally accompanied by the sanshin (a three-stringed lute) and drums.
A critical element is the yubi-bue, or finger whistling, which provides sharp rhythmic accents.
Listen for the Sanshin, Drum, Yubi-bue (finger whistle).
The pulse is 2/4 or 4/4 at about 160 beats a minute.
A high-energy sound dominated by the bright, percussive twang of the sanshin and the sharp, piercing interruptions of finger whistling. The tempo often increases toward a frantic, joyful climax.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Kachāshī is performed in various settings including weddings, festivals, and victory celebrations.
While often danced in casual attire during spontaneous celebrations, traditional Okinawan dress is common at formal festivals.
The dance typically occurs in open communal spaces where large groups can gather and 'mix.'

scenes.title: The people
narration: While primarily associated with Okinawa, specific songs like 'Amakawa bushi' and 'Takoo-yama' suggest variations in mood and purpose across different local contexts within the Ryūkyū archipelago.
Kachāshī is a distinct branch of Ryūkyūan folk dance, separate from the more formal court dances of the Ryūkyū Kingdom, emphasizing improvisation and communal participation.
